opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really the core tension. Every time you make something cheaper, whether that's swapping in a smaller model, trimming context, caching more aggressively, or cutting steps out of the loop, you're implicitly betting that the thing you removed wasn't load-bearing. Evaluation is how you check that bet instead of just hoping.

The way I think about it, the first step is being honest about what "the task" actually is. It's easy to measure something convenient, like whether the output looks well-formed or whether some benchmark score holds steady, and miss what users care about. So we try to anchor on end-to-end outcomes: did the system get the right answer, did it complete the workflow, would a person accept the result without having to redo it. Proxy metrics are useful for fast iteration, but you have to keep validating that they still track the real outcome. Cost changes are exactly the kind of thing that can quietly break that correlation.

Second, you want a fixed eval set you trust, and you compare the before and after on the same inputs. That sounds obvious, but the details matter. Run things multiple times, because these systems are stochastic and a one-point difference can easily be noise. Look at the distribution, not just the average. A change can keep the mean flat while making the hard cases much worse, and the hard cases are often the ones that matter most.

That leads to the third thing, which is to deliberately stratify by difficulty and by type of input. Cost optimizations tend to be fine on the easy, common cases and fail on the long tail: longer inputs, ambiguous requests, the cases where the system actually needed that extra reasoning step or the extra context you just cut. So we carve out slices for those and watch them specifically. If the easy slice holds and the hard slice drops, that's a real regression even if the overall number barely moves.

Fourth, I like doing a lot of diffing at the level of individual examples. Take the cases where the old and new versions disagree and actually read them. Aggregate metrics tell you whether something changed. Reading the disagreements tells you why, and often you'll find the cheaper version is failing in a systematic way you can fix cheaply, or occasionally that it's actually better and your grader was wrong.

And finally, offline eval only gets you so far. Once something passes, we prefer rolling it out gradually and watching real-world signals, whether that's retries, user corrections, escalations, or whatever the domain-specific signal of failure is. Production traffic always has stuff your eval set didn't anticipate.

So the short version is: define success in terms of the real outcome, compare like-for-like with enough repetitions to beat noise, pay special attention to the hard tail, read the actual differences, and treat deployment as the last stage of the eval rather than the end of it. The goal isn't "no change at all," it's knowing exactly what you traded away and deciding it was worth it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly the question that keeps me up at night more than any of the clever caching or routing tricks themselves. Because the failure mode here is really insidious. If you make the system cheaper and it just breaks, that's fine, you notice immediately. The scary case is when you make it cheaper and it gets subtly worse, and nobody notices for three weeks until a customer tells you.

So the way we think about it is basically in layers. The first layer is we never ship a cost optimization without a frozen eval set that represents the actual task distribution. Not synthetic prompts we made up, but a sample of real traffic, with graded outcomes. And the key word is frozen. The temptation is always to tweak the eval when the new version looks slightly worse, and you have to resist that, because then you're just grading on a curve.

The second layer is we treat cost and quality as a Pareto frontier rather than a single number. So every change gets plotted. Did we move left on cost? Did we move down on quality? And how much? Because sometimes a 40% cost reduction with a half-percent quality regression is absolutely worth it, and sometimes a 10% cost reduction that quietly drops your hardest tail cases is a disaster, even though on average it looks fine. Averages hide a lot. We look at the worst decile very closely.

The third thing, and this is the one people skip, is that the eval has to be task-grounded rather than output-grounded. A lot of these optimizations, like aggressive context truncation or routing to a smaller model for "easy" steps, produce outputs that still look fluent and reasonable. A judge model will happily say "yes, this is a good response." But did it actually accomplish the thing? Did the code run? Did the agent reach the end state? So wherever we can, we check the outcome in the world, not the text.

And then the last piece is just humility about distribution shift. Your eval set is a snapshot. The traffic drifts. So we keep a small slice of production running through the expensive path as a continuous control group, and we diff against it. It costs a little, but it's the only way to know whether the savings are still real six months later.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to evaluate cost and task success together. If you make something cheaper but it no longer does the task, that’s not really a saving. So I’d start with a baseline: on a representative set of tasks, how often does the system succeed, and what does it cost to get a successful result? Then you can make a change and compare those same outcomes.

The tricky part is defining success. For something with a verifiable outcome, you can check it directly. For more open-ended tasks, you need a rubric and some human judgment. And I’d look closely at the failures, not just the average score. You want to know whether you’ve made the system broadly more efficient or whether you’ve made it cheaper by giving up on the harder tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to evaluate the cost savings and the quality together. Making a run cheaper isn’t useful if it stops completing the task. So I’d start with a baseline on representative tasks, make the change, and compare the outcomes. Did it finish? Was the result correct? Did it need more retries or more human intervention?

And I’d look at individual failures, not just the average score. You can preserve average performance while getting much worse on a particular kind of task. The metric I care about is cost per successfully completed task, including the recovery work, rather than just cost per model call.
